Operator:  
Good morning, and welcome to the Voltara Motors Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are currently in a listen-only mode. After the speakers’ presentation, there will be a question and answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star then one on your touchtone phone. To withdraw your question, press star then two. As a reminder, this conference call is being recorded.  

I would now like to turn the conference over to Emily Carter, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.  

Emily Carter:  
Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Voltara Motors' Q2 2024 earnings call. Joining me today are Alex Rivera, CEO; Sarah Chen, CFO; and other members of our leadership team.  

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that today's discussion may contain forward-looking statements that are subject to risks and uncertainties. Actual results may differ materially from those expressed or implied by these statements. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.  

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Alex Rivera.  

Alex Rivera:  
Thank you, Emily, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. Q2 was a pivotal quarter for Voltara Motors. We made significant strides in key areas, including robust changes in our order backlog and reservation trends signaling strong demand, improved gross margins per vehicle through cost efficiencies and premium mix shifts, record delivery volumes across models and regions amid production ramps, and accelerated charging network expansion with rising utilization rates. We are particularly excited about the upcoming ramp of our V6 mid-size pickup and its anticipated boost to our market share in the high-volume truck segment.  

These achievements position us strongly in the competitive EV landscape, where we're leveraging vertical integration from our Nevada Gigafactory to software-defined vehicles. Now, I'll turn the call over to Sarah to discuss our financial performance in more detail.  

Sarah Chen:  
Thank you, Alex. Good morning, everyone. For Q2 2024, our revenue reached $2.85 billion, representing a 52% increase year-over-year, driven by scaled deliveries and favorable product mix. Our gross margin expanded to 24.8%, up 420 basis points from last year, reflecting manufacturing efficiencies and battery cost reductions. Operating expenses were $520 million, including increased R&D for next-gen autonomy. Net income came in at $185 million, or $0.42 per diluted share. We are maintaining a strong balance sheet with $3.4 billion in cash and cash equivalents, providing ample runway for our CapEx plans. Our guidance for Q3 is revenue of $3.6 to $3.9 billion, deliveries of 210,000 to 220,000 vehicles, and continued margin expansion toward 26%.  

Let me dive deeper into some of our most critical leading indicators, starting with changes in our order backlog and reservation trends. As you know, in the EV industry, backlog represents our unfulfilled customer orders—those firm commitments with deposits or financing approvals—while reservations are our refundable expressions of interest, often tied to pre-orders for upcoming models. These metrics give us real-time visibility into demand elasticity, production pacing, and our competitive positioning against peers like Tesla, Rivian, and BYD.  

As of June 30th, our global order backlog stood at $18.7 billion, up 22% sequentially from $15.3 billion at the end of Q1, and a robust 45% year-over-year. This equates to approximately 285,000 units at current average selling prices, or ASPs, providing us with over 12 months of visibility at our Q2 production run rate of 22,000 vehicles per month. On the reservation front, we ended the quarter with 420,000 global reservations, a 15% increase quarter-over-quarter and 28% year-over-year. Excluding cancellations, net reservation adds totaled 95,000 in Q2 alone—our strongest quarter since the Voltara V8 SUV launch in late 2022.  

Breaking this down by product line, our flagship V8 SUV continues to drive the backlog surge. V8 orders now represent 62% of the total backlog, up from 55% last quarter, with 175,000 units pending delivery. This reflects the model's strong resonance post our April pricing adjustment—we reduced the base V8 MSRP by $4,500 to $54,900, unlocking price-sensitive demand without eroding margins, thanks to our 4680 cell cost reductions from the Nevada Gigafactory ramp. ASPs held steady at $62,200, supported by 85% take rates on our $12,000 Ultima autonomy package, which bundles L4-capable hardware akin to Tesla's FSD.  

Our new V6 mid-size pickup, launched in March, is the real breakout star on reservations. We've accumulated 210,000 reservations since reveal, converting 18% to firm orders in Q2—ahead of our 12-15% internal target. Backlog for V6 sits at $4.2 billion, or 68,000 units, fueled by fleet deals with Amazon and UPS totaling 15,000 units under the IRA's commercial clean vehicle credit. Meanwhile, our entry-level V4 hatchback saw softer trends, with backlog flat at 42,000 units, as we prioritize higher-margin V6 production. Reservations here dipped 5% due to waitlist fatigue, but we're addressing this with a Q3 'V4 Boost' campaign offering free fast-charging credits.  

Regionally, the picture is bifurcated but overwhelmingly positive. North America remains our fortress, accounting for 68% of backlog at $12.7 billion—up 28% QoQ—driven by $7,500 point-of-sale IRA rebates and leasing penetration hitting 42% of deliveries. US reservations grew 20% to 285,000, with Texas and California leading at 45% share, bolstered by our new Laredo Gigafactory hitting 40 GWh annual output. Europe contributed 22% of backlog, or $4.1 billion, up 18% QoQ despite softening BEV subsidies in Germany post the €9,000 KBA scrappage incentive phase-out. Our Berlin plant's 2170-to-4680 cell transition has de-risked supply, enabling 25,000 unit deliveries YTD. China, at 8% of backlog or $1.5 billion, faced headwinds from BYD's Seagull price war—reservations there grew just 5%, but we're countering with localized LFP packs from our Shanghai JV, targeting sub-$30,000 ASPs by year-end. Emerging markets like Australia and Southeast Asia added 2% incrementally via right-hand-drive V8 exports.  

What’s driving these trends? First, production execution: Q2 output rose 35% YoY to 66,000 vehicles, with gross margins expanding on scale and vertical integration—we're now 75% in-sourced on battery packs versus 45% a year ago. Second, technical initiatives like our Over-the-Air 'Voltara Neural' update in May, which boosted reservation conversions by 12% via enhanced ADAS demos. Third, strategic pricing and incentives: dynamic pricing algorithms, similar to Tesla's, adjusted for 15% of orders, while our $99/month leasing for V4 captured Gen Z demand.  

Looking ahead, we expect Q3 backlog to grow another 15-20% to $21-22 billion, supported by V6 ramp to 10,000/month and initial CyberVault semi-truck reservations opening in September. Risks include supply chain volatility in cathode materials—we've hedged 80% of 2024 NCM needs—and potential US tariff hikes on LFP imports. Strategically, we're doubling down on software margins, now at 65% gross, and energy storage cross-sells, with 25% of V8 owners adding Wallbox units. This backlog fortress positions us for $2.5 billion in Q4 free cash flow, funding our $5 billion CapEx plan for gigacasting and next-gen solid-state cells by 2026.  

Building on this demand visibility, let's turn to our delivery volumes by model and geographic region, which directly tie into production ramps, supply chain execution, and those robust demand signals. In Q2 2024, we delivered a record 187,500 vehicles globally, up 28% year-over-year from 146,200 in Q2 2023, and 12% quarter-over-quarter from 167,300 in Q1 2024. This marks our 10th consecutive quarter of YoY growth, driven by the Shanghai Gigafactory ramp on our V8 SUV crossover and initial V6 pickup deliveries from our Nevada facility. Average selling price held steady at $48,200, reflecting a healthy mix shift toward higher-margin models like the V8 and V6, offsetting some price adjustments in entry-level segments to counter BYD and legacy OEM pressure.  

Our portfolio delivered strong across the board, with SUVs and trucks leading—now 68% of total volume, up from 55% a year ago, aligning with consumer preferences for versatile platforms amid rising fuel costs and IRA incentives. The V4 compact sedan delivered 52,000 units, +15% YoY, flat QoQ. This workhorse continues to anchor our mass-market segment at ~28% of total deliveries. Production efficiency hit 99% OEE at Fremont, thanks to our 4680 cell integration, which reduced pack costs by 18% YoY. Demand softened slightly in Europe due to subsidy phase-outs, but FSD take rates climbed to 32% here, boosting recurring high-margin software revenue.  

The V8 mid-size SUV was our star performer at 89,000 units, +42% YoY, +18% QoQ—47% of mix. Shanghai output exceeded 5,000/week, with structural battery packs enabling a 10% range boost to 520 EPA miles on the Long Range variant. This model's 65% gross margin underscores our vertical integration edge over competitors like the Tesla Model Y or VW ID.4. The V6 luxury pickup variant delivered 21,500 units, +35% YoY, +8% QoQ at 11% of mix. High-performance deliveries surged 50% on 1,020 hp output and sub-2-second 0-60, appealing to enterprise fleets. OTA updates for unsupervised FSD drove 45% attach rates, with enterprise ADAS contracts up 60% YoY.  

The V6 full-size pickup hit 25,000 units, our first full quarter post-launch—13% of mix. Ramp challenges from stainless steel exoskeleton supply eased, hitting 1,200/week by quarter-end. Towing capacity at 14,000 lbs and 500+ mile range positioned it well against Ford F-150 Lightning and Rivian R1T, capturing 22% US pickup market share in the EV segment per Cox Automotive data. Emerging platforms like our V-Van for commercial fleets added 4,000 pilot units, teeing up Q3 scaling with Amazon and UPS partnerships.  

Shifting to geography, North America remains our fortress at 112,000 deliveries—60% of total, +32% YoY. US volumes hit 98,000, fueled by $7,500 IRA tax credits pushing V8 to 55,000 units—overtaking Tesla's Q2 US crossover lead per SNE Research. Canada added 14,000, with Quebec incentives driving fleet adoption. Europe contributed 38,500 units—21% of total, +22% YoY but -5% QoQ due to German subsidy cuts and softening UK demand. V8 dominated at 24,000 units, with right-hand-drive ramps in Berlin Gigafactory boosting localization to 85%. Norway remains a bright spot at 12% penetration of new EV sales, while France and Netherlands grew 40% on urban delivery mandates. We're countering headwinds with a €2B price-lock program and LFP battery localization to dodge tariffs.  

China was our growth engine at 28,000 units—15% of total, +65% YoY from Shanghai Giga's 95% capacity utilization. V4 and V8 captured 8% local sedan/crossover share, narrowing the gap with BYD's Seagull and NIO ET5 despite 125% tariff headwinds. Export volumes to APAC ex-China rose 30% to 6,000, targeting Japan and Australia with V6 demos. Rest of World rounded out at 9,000 units—5%, +50% YoY, led by Mexico Gigafactory pilots (2,500 units) and Middle East fleet deals (3,000 V6s for oilfield ops). Regionally, mix shifts are telling: NA skewed premium (V6 25% of regional mix), Europe mass-market (V4/V8 80%), and China volume-focused (V4 60%). Inventory days on hand improved to 45 from 62 YoY, signaling demand outpacing supply.  

These results validate our 'Gigafactory Everywhere' playbook—Q3 guidance calls for 210,000-220,000 deliveries, with V6 hitting 2,500/week and V-Van entering volume. Key initiatives include 4680 cell yields at 92% (unlocking 20% cost savings), Robotaxi unveil in October to juice FSD monetization, and Mexico Giga ramp for NAFTA tariff-proofing. We're also eyeing India entry via Tata partnership to tap 30M annual auto demand. Demand remains robust—global waitlists at 450,000, with 75% for next-gen platforms. Risks include supply chain silicon carbide constraints and China price wars, but our 25% YoY energy storage growth (12 GWh deployed) provides a margin buffer.  

Next, a key profitability metric: gross margin per vehicle, calculated as our average selling price per vehicle minus the cost of goods sold per vehicle, expressed on a per-unit basis. This strips out fixed overheads like SG&A and R&D, giving a clear line of sight into manufacturing economics and scalability—critical in the EV landscape where battery costs and supply chain volatility can swing margins by thousands overnight.  

In Q2, we delivered a record gross margin per vehicle of $13,200, up 28% year-over-year from $10,300 in Q2 2023, and 9% sequentially from $12,100 in Q1. This puts us on par with Tesla's recent Model Y margins in the mid-teens, while lapping legacy OEMs below $8,000. On a fleet-wide basis, this translated to our 24.7% gross margin—our highest ever—driven by 187,500 vehicle deliveries, a 65% YoY increase.  

ASP expansion fueled this: Q2 ASP at $48,700, up 12% YoY, from a richer product mix. Premium trims like the V8 SUV, with its 100 kWh NMC battery pack and 500+ mile EPA range, accounted for 42% of volume—up from 28% last year—commanding a $15,000 ASP premium versus V4. Strong uptake on our Performance Pack, bundling 800V architecture for 350 kW DC charging, added $4,200 to ASP without hiking COGS much. Pricing discipline held despite BYD pressure in Europe; we focused on FOMO for OTA-upgradable Full Autonomy Hardware 3.0.  

On COGS—the margin battleground—we shaved $2,800 per vehicle YoY to $35,500. Battery costs, ~45% of COGS, dropped 22% to $16,000 per pack, via Nevada Gigafactory 2 at 95% utilization, ramping 4680 cells 15% cheaper than suppliers. LFP for V4 models—mirroring CATL blade tech with silicon anode doping for 10% higher density—slashed cathode costs 30% vs. NMC. Lithium carbonate down 45% YoY to $12,000/ton juiced this.  

Manufacturing efficiencies: direct labor to $1,200/vehicle via AI-optimized giga-press lines at 8,000-ton capacity, casting underbody in one piece like Tesla's unboxed process—cutting SKU complexity 40% and assembly to under 10 hours. Supply chain wins: multi-year nickel sulfate offtakes at $18,000/ton from Indonesia, hedging LME volatility; Panasonic 2170 as bridge to in-house 4680 H1 2025.  

Regionally: North America (58% volume) at $15,400/vehicle, boosted by IRA 30D credits averaging $7,500, plus $4,000 45Z for fleets to Hertz/Uber; Texas Giga at 92% utilization. Europe (25%) at $11,200 due to VAT taper and VW/Stellantis pricing, but Berlin localization (70% EU content) mitigated tariffs. China/APAC (17%) at $10,800 vs. BYD Seagull; Shanghai JV at 30,000 units/month with local LFP for 18% lower COGS.  

We're targeting $18,000+ by YE 2025 via 4680 ramp to 50 GWh ($90/kWh packs), $99/month Ride Autonomy subs lifting effective ASP, 60% premium mix with 2025 Odyssey rival, and USMCA recycling for 20% black mass recovery. Risks like cobalt spikes or IRA changes, but 85% mineral coverage positions us well. This compounding metric paves FCF positivity in Q4 and 25%+ EBITDA in 2026.  

Finally, our charging network expansion and utilization rates are pivotal to retention, fleets, and revenue diversification—contributing 12% of recurring services revenue, up from 8% YoY. In Q2, we deployed 1,250 new DC fast-charging stalls across 185 sites, bringing global total to 4,200 stalls—a 42% YoY increase, ahead of 15,000 YE24 guidance. This includes 500 NACS-compatible stalls post our Tesla interoperability announcement. Prioritized high-traffic: 65% NA new on I-5/I-10/I-95, 95% permitting via PG&E/Edison ties.  

North America: 72% additions (900 stalls), 48% utilization from V8's 22% premium share. Europe: 320 stalls in Germany/Netherlands/Norway for ED-S amid AFIR mandates; regulatory delays offset by ISO 15118-20 pilots. Asia-Pacific: 30 Shanghai stalls at 35% utilization for fleets, eyeing MIIT's 1.2M chargers.  

Utilization hit 41% average—up 18% QoQ, 62% YoY—beating Tesla's 35-40%, Electrify America's 28%. Peak (4-8 PM) at 72% in LA/Berlin via dynamic pricing ($0.28-$0.52/kWh), ARPU $1.42 (+25% YoY). Idle time 12% via AI Stall Optimizer and ED OS 4.2 preconditioning (85% fleet).  

Technical: 40% new V3.5 Ultra-Fast at 400kW (200 miles/12 min for 800V); V2G/V2L pilots at 50 CA sites ($0.15/kWh credits). NACS adapters onboarded 25k non-Voltara vehicles; IONNA/ChargePoint roaming adds 12,000 stalls.  

This moat generated $18M Q2 cash flow at 65% gross—EBITDA positive above 30%. Targeting 50% mid-2025 via Amazon's 5,000 V8 commitment. H2 Capex $450M from $3.4B cash, 28% IRR. Q3: 1,800 stalls, 45% FY24 utilization. Risks: grid via 500MW VPP; comp from EVgo. With 18% US EV sales, primed for 3x scale by 2027.  

Now, I'll hand the call back to the operator for the Q&A session.  

Operator:  
Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star then one. Our first question comes from Mike Johnson with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.  

Analyst 1:  
Thanks, and congrats on a strong quarter. Sarah, on the backlog growth, how sustainable is the V6 reservation conversion, especially with fleet deals, and any update on CyberVault pre-orders?  

Alex Rivera:  
Great question, Mike. The V6 conversion at 18% exceeds targets thanks to fleet validations from Amazon and UPS, leveraging IRA credits—their multi-year commitments provide sticky volume. CyberVault reservations open September, early software previews via Voltara Neural are generating buzz, with initial fleet interest from logistics peers. We're confident in 15-20% backlog growth this Q3.  

Operator:  
Our next question from Lisa Patel with Morgan Stanley.  

Analyst 2:  
Sarah, impressive gross margins per vehicle—can you elaborate on the LFP qualification timeline for V8 and regional COGS sensitivities to mineral prices?  

Sarah Chen:  
Thanks, Lisa. LFP qualification for base V8 trims starts Q4 pilots, full ramp H1 2025 with 20% cost edge via silicon doping—already in V4. Regional COGS resilient: NA benefits from IRA passthroughs, Europe from localization, China from JV scale. We've hedged 85% minerals, so even with lithium volatility, we see $15k+ NA margins holding.  

Operator:  
Next from David Lee with JPMorgan.  

Analyst 3:  
Alex, delivery mix shifted premium—thoughts on Europe softening, and how does charging utilization tie into V6 fleet retention?  

Alex Rivera:  
David, Europe deliveries grew 22% YoY despite subsidies; price-lock and LFP localization counter VW pressure. Charging utilization at 41% average, peaking 72%, directly boosts retention—V6 fleets like Amazon see 80% corridor loading via V2G pilots, enhancing TCO and loyalty.  

Emily Carter:  
Thank you for your questions. We have time for one more.  

Operator:  
Our final question from Rachel Kim with Barclays.  

Analyst 4:  
Sarah, on charging expansion, what's the CapEx payback model with NACS, and utilization risks from third-party roaming?  

Sarah Chen:  
Rachel, NACS accelerates payback—our 500 stalls already at 48% NA utilization, with roaming adding 12k stalls via IONNA equity. Model assumes 10% annual growth to 28% IRR; fleets guarantee loads. Risks low—AI optimizer cuts idle, VPP mitigates grid—targeting 50% mid-2025.  

Operator:  
Thank you. I would now like to turn the call back to Alex Rivera for closing remarks.  

Alex Rivera:  
Thank you, operator, and thank you all for joining us today. We are confident that Voltara Motors is well-positioned for continued success in the rapidly evolving automotive landscape. We look forward to updating you on our progress next quarter.  

Emily Carter:  
Thank you for joining us today. This concludes the Voltara Motors Q2 2024 earnings call. You may now disconnect.
